::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .36", Sentence = "The correlation between the change in score and sex was not significant, rpb(19) = -.21, p = .36, 2-tails,0 = male,1 = female."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: LEGO® Serious Play® (LSP) is a methodology designed to help individuals and groups engage in meaningful problem-solving and communication as they address a variety of individual and organizational challenges.
An LSP intervention was designed to help undergraduate students gain experience in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics.

Results revealed that the intervention significantly increased students' self-reported experience of expressing a Christian perspective on ethics (Mdifference = .54, SDdifference = .68, d = .80, p < .001).

text.text: The results suggest that LSP can effectively facilitate student experience in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics and can potentially contribute to other learning outcomes.

LSP is a methodology designed to facilitate thinking around intangible concepts, enhance group communication, and promote problem-solving in a variety of organizational settings (Kristiansen & Rasmussen, 2014).

text.text: In an educational environment, LSP could be described as a pedagogy because its content can be customized to support specific learning outcomes.

Functionally, LSP begins with a carefully crafted prompt aligned with the learning outcomes, followed by building a model using LEGO® bricks in response to the prompt and sharing an explanation of the model in a group setting.
LSP has been used in business, education, nonprofit, government, church, and military settings, both in small and large group environments (Dykes, 2018).

text.text: A core principle of LSP is enabling 100% participation (Rasmussen Consulting, n.d.), which means that every individual in every group must contribute to the group activities of constructing individual models with LEGO® bricks and then discussing their meaning.
This way, all participants have an equal opportunity to share their models and perspectives associated with the prompt.
The required participation of everyone can be particularly important in settings where organizational superiors are present, or some participants are dominant or excessively talkative.

LSP has been shown to create a "level-playing-field" through this required sharing (McCusker, 2014). McCusker (2020) found that LSP helped achieve authentic, non-hierarchical communication leading to new insights, a description of participatory learning. Cerezo-Narvaez et al. (2019) also noted that it generated communication resulting in opportunities from an individual point-of-view, through a relaxed, fun approach that generated involvement.

text.text: This methodology creates a safe environment to share ideas about the topic under discussion.

We hypothesize that students will have self-report having greater experience expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics after a properly designed LSP intervention than before the intervention.
Such a goal aligns with the learning outcomes of many undergraduate business courses at Christian universities.

A quantitative pre-experimental study utilizing a survey-based pretest-posttest design was conducted in an upper-division business ethics class at a Christian university in Southern California that does not require a profession of Christian faith from the students.
The purpose of this study was to understand whether participation in a LSP intervention can help students gain measurable experience in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics.
One section of a required ethics course for business majors, consisting of upper-division undergraduate students, provided data before and after the LSP intervention.
The quantitative data came from a pretest and a posttest.
The pretest (a survey measuring the participants' selfreported experience with expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics) was conducted at the end of Week 4 of a 16-week semester.
The posttest (an identical survey) was conducted at the beginning of Week 8 of the same semester.
The intervention was administered between the pretest and posttest, during Weeks 5, 6, and 7.
The intervention consisted of six 85-minute class sessions during this period.
After the post-test, students participated in small group interviews to debrief.
These interviews provided additional insight into their experiences during the intervention.
Participants were upper-division (typically in their final year) undergraduate students with a business-related major.
All participants were 18 years or older.
Although the LSP intervention was part of the required coursework assigned in the syllabus, participation in the pretest and posttest was optional.
The right of the students to opt out of the pre-and/or posttest was communicated multiple times.
The research project received Institutional Review Board review and students provided their informed consent before participating.

The consent provided clear instructions on the purpose of the study, the rights of participants, steps that had been taken to ensure confidentiality, and actions that could be taken by participants if they had questions or concerns about anything associated with the study.
This included contact information for the institution's Research Integrity Officer.

It is reasonable to suggest that the academically based power relationship between the instructor and students, along with the culture of the Christian university setting, might solicit outcomes that did not reflect autonomy.

To mitigate this risk, participants were told multiple times (both verbally and in writing) that while the intervention itself was a required class activity, their responses would not be graded and would not have any impact on the outcome of the course.
All 25 students in the class participated in the intervention and the anonymous, online survey-based pretest/posttest after providing their informed consent.
However, only 21 participants provided codes (the last 4 digits of their phone numbers) in the pretest that could be matched to the codes that they provided in the posttest.
The only demographic information collected was sex.
Of the 21 participants with usable data, 12 were female, and 9 were male.
The LSP intervention consisted of 6 class sessions, each led by 2-3 certified and experienced LSP facilitators.
The participants were divided into four groups of approximately six students, ensuring that all participants would have adequate time to share their ideas.

In LSP, a build consists of a verbal or written prompt provided by the facilitators, a time for building during which each participant uses LEGO® bricks to respond to the prompt, and a time for sharing the meaning of what one has built with other participants in one's group.
Builds are sometimes followed by a time where a spokesperson from each group shares with the other groups what his or her group experienced.
Throughout the six sessions, the facilitators followed the prescribed LSP protocol.
This protocol includes initial builds to familiarize participants with the LSP method, while also building trust among group members and with the facilitators.
The facilitators encouraged communication, valued contributions, and ensured every individual and group had adequate opportunities to share.
The facilitators also issued appropriate challenges to ideas, which provided further opportunities for participants to reflect on and share their respective models.
For each session, participants changed groups to experience a greater variety of perspectives.
The first session was not related to the intervention's main content.
As prescribed in LSP, the goal of this session was to familiarize participants with the LSP method and process (Kristiansen & Rasmussen, 2014).
text.formatted: As prescribed in LSP, the goal of this session was to familiarize participants with the LSP method and process <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kristiansen & Rasmussen, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The following sessions included case studies and ethical dilemmas that participants might encounter in a workplace setting.
Topics included how participants would handle the responsibility of remote work positions when unsupervised, and how they would react to co-workers who violated company rules.
Each build included several minutes of constructing a model, followed by brief opportunities for all participants to individually share the meaning of their models.
During the final session, the facilitators encouraged participants to express their beliefs concerning a Christian perspective on business ethics.
Participants were asked to participate in builds that were introduced by these prompts: 1.
Build a model of your personal Christian business ethics worldview.
Add some ethical challenges faced by Christians in business ethics.
Do not propose solutions at this point.
Adapt your model to include your worldview, challenges, and how you will guard against those challenges in the future.
As with prior builds, each participant was instructed to verbally describe their model to their small group.
The full details of the six sessions, including all the build prompts, are found in Appendix A.

For both the pretest and posttest, the Experience Discussing a Christian Perspective on Ethics Scale was used to measure the degree to which the participants saw themselves as having experience discussing expressing a Christian perspective on ethics in workplace settings.

This ad hoc scale, created for this study, consists of 8 Likert items such as "I have experience explaining to others what it means to have a Christian perspective on business ethics" and "I have experience explaining how I would act ethically from a Christian perspective when new situations arise" (1 = strongly disagree,5 = strongly agree).
The items were chosen because of their face validity and were reviewed by subject matter experts who had experience teaching undergraduate and graduate business ethics courses.

The focus was on measuring the students' experience (not confidence, self-efficacy, or perceived competence) in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics, which mapped into the learning outcome of "express a Christian perspective on business ethics."
See Appendix B for the complete scale.
In addition to having high face validity, Cronbach's coefficient of reliability for the scale was high (𝛼 = .89).
Participants verbally shared their experience during small group interviews with six to eight participants each, which were conducted after the intervention and the posttest.
The participants were randomly divided into three groups, and each group was led by one of the facilitators who conducted the intervention.
This increased rapport and leveraged existing relationships of trust that had been built over the previous weeks.
Students were not required to answer questions, but facilitators encouraged participation and utilized a discussion format in presenting the questions.
Six questions were presented to the participants, who could respond to the degree that they desired: 1.
Tell me what it means to have a Christian perspective on business ethics.
How would you explain to people how you personally apply a Christian perspective to business ethics?
Do you feel prepared to make ethical decisions in the workplace?
Explain.
Are there ethical challenges in the workplace that you do not feel prepared to face?
If so, please describe them.
Looking back at the activities and the discussions, what is your biggest takeaway about business ethics?
How do you see your faith influencing the way you approach ethical decisions in business?
Responses to the six questions were recorded by facilitators and then consolidated into a shared spreadsheet.

To test the hypothesis that participants would have self-report having increased more experience expressing a Christian perspective on ethics after the intervention than before, both a pretest test score (M = 3.43, SD = .54) and a posttest score (M = 3.97, SD = .67) was calculated for each participant by averaging their responses to the 8 items on the Experience Discussing a Christian Perspective on Ethics Scale (Appendix B).

A paired two-sample t-test comparing the means indicated that participants, as hypothesized, perceived they had significantly increased experience expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics after the intervention than before, t(20) = 3.66, p < .001, 1-tail.

However, the preexperimental design used does not allow for claims of causation.
There was no significant evidence that the intervention affected males and females differently.
The correlation between the change in score and sex was not significant, rpb(19) = -.21, p = .36, 2-tails,0 = male,1 = female.
A consistent theme from the small group discussions included an increased sense of confidence in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics.

Moreover, perhaps because of increased confidence, participants indicated that they believed common ground on ethical issues is often possible and that individuals can agree on the right thing to do, even when approaching situations from different perspectives.
Participants acknowledged their lack of professional experience and that true tests of their conviction would occur as they encountered ethical quandaries in professional life.
In addition, participants noted that ethical decisions are complicated and that listening to other perspectives may be required.
Participants also noted the need to connect theory with practice.

An example response was, "I think the biggest takeaway I took was when we're talking about ethics, we kind of tend to think these things are just theoretical and won't actually happen in everyday life, but it's important to prepare yourself for these everyday situations and to continue to practice these seemingly theoretical problems."
Overall, the content of the group interviews was consistent with the quantitative results.
Students expressed the perception that they gained experience in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics.

This study examined whether a carefully designed LSP intervention could increase would be associated with an increase in students' self-reported experience in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics.
A pretest-posttest survey showed that the six-session LSP intervention was perceived by students to greatly increase their experience in this domain.

Information shared during the small group debriefing interviews was congruent with this outcome, as participants verbally indicated that the intervention gave them notably greater confidence and experience in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics.
This project was a standalone study, but it followed a previous study that also measured the effectiveness of LSP (Dykes McGehee et al., 2024).

text.text: Post-intervention interviews from the first study indicated that the students had considered ideas relevant to vocational identity, but the pretest-posttest data showed no significant change in the learning outcome, namely, a more defined sense of vocational identity.
The reasons for the null results are speculative.
However, inadequate preparation of the participant group, flaws in the intervention design, and a lack of life experience among the participants may have contributed.
For this study, the authors revised the design process and incorporated lessons learned from the first study.
These revisions appear to have contributed to the success of the current LSP intervention.
In addition to the quantitative results, the information shared during the debriefing discussions indicated that the intervention was successful.
This was not the case in the first study.

In the previous study (Dykes McGehee et al., 2024), which aimed to develop students' vocational identity through an LSP intervention, participants were not provided with preintervention content on the subject matter.

text.text: The decision not to include preparation material was intentional, as it was hypothesized that presenting such content might bias participants' perspectives.

While this decision was made with good intentions, the lack of life experience and understanding of the concept may have made the LSP intervention difficult for students to understand and apply to their vocational identity.
In contrast, participants in the current study received four weeks of traditional classroom instruction before the workshop, providing a context where scaffolding of concepts was possible.

This included introductions to ethical theories, law, and policy, along with a variety of marketrelevant case studies, which provided a framework for understanding the content of the LSP intervention.
The introductory lessons also included small group discussions of case studies, which may have made it easier for participants to engage with and benefit from the LSP intervention.

The concept of scaffolding draws on Vygotsky's (1978) Zone of Proximal Development, which suggests that students learn most effectively when new concepts are intentionally connected to what they already know.

text.text: It is reasonable to suggest that the ethical decision-making models grounded in Christian values and organizational principles presented prior to the workshop provided a shared foundation.
LSP was then used to help students work through realistic workplace situations, allowing them to translate theory into practice.

It appears that the main reason for the significant results in this study (in contrast to the previous study, Dykes McGehee et al., 2024) is that the LSP intervention and the learning outcome measured (experience expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics) were closely aligned.

text.text: Another factor that appears to have contributed to the success of this study was the careful design of the LSP interventions.

Most of the six sessions of the intervention began with a skills-building exercise designed to engage students with the LSP methodology and expose them to new idea concepts that could be expressed with LSP (See the warm-up build prompts in Appendix A).

While participants displayed increasing comfort and familiarity with the process throughout the three-week intervention, these first builds in each session may have helped students recall material from prior sessions and re-engage quickly with the LSP process.
Moving from the case study builds to the more personal builds may have helped participants become more comfortable sharing their own perspectives.

Finally, as students moved from creating individual models to collaborating on shared builds by merging and adapting their personal models, they developed a better understanding of how to express a Christian perspective of ethics through these verbal and hands-on interactions.

In addition to experience expressing a Christian perspective of business ethics, students may have strengthened their ethical judgment, organizational awareness, and sense of responsibility, all of which are competencies required for effective management and ethical behavior in organizational settings.
This study has demonstrated that LSP may be used to achieve the desired learning outcomes through a well-designed series of prompts that closely align with those outcomes.

Because of the versatility of LEGO® bricks and figures, LSP activities are easily adaptable to Christian contexts.
Christianity often addresses abstract concepts (e.g., the non-material world, faith, love, and service), and LSP enables students to think more concretely about them.
Such activities are not limited to business classes but can be used in any class that deals with abstract ideas.
A pre-experimental design, such as that used in this study, cannot demonstrate that the intervention caused the change in the outcome.

Because Christian institutions often provide multiple concurrent programs that contribute to an individual's personal growth (Dunaetz, 2025), we cannot be sure that the increase in experience expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics is due to the LSP intervention.

text.text: More specifically, lectures, discussion, reflection, and case studies in other classes taken at the same time limit the ability to specifically attribute outcomes to the LSP intervention.
Nevertheless, the results suggest that the intervention had a statistically significant impact and is therefore an intriguing pedagogical activity for future study and application.
The participants in the study were full-time students at a private, Christian university that has intentionally designed a holistic development experience for all students.

These experiences include faith-integrated curriculum, dedicated Bible classes, required chapel attendance, and a myriad of opportunities to participate in faith-integrated extracurricular activities, all of which may provide students with the opportunity to discuss business ethics from a Christian perspective.
The study was conducted with one group of participants and did not include a control or comparison group.
A future study that includes a control group may allow researchers to more effectively isolate the impact of LSP intervention.
However, the intervention effect size was large, and there were only 4 weeks between the pretest and posttest, providing evidence that at least part of the outcome was due to the intervention.
A follow-up study could examine whether increased experience expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics leads to more consistent ethical behavior in professional settings.
In addition, researchers could study not only perceptions of expression, but also competency development.
LSP is increasingly used in higher education.
Its constructivist and constructionist pedagogy is adaptable to any course that deals with abstract ideas that should apply to real-life situations.
This study has demonstrated that a well-designed LSP activity may contribute to accomplishing the learning outcomes in a business ethics class in a Christian university.
